design_detail: Systematic review without meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024530359; PRISMA 2020 cited) of studies of physical exercise in people with methamphetamine use disorder reporting negative mood (anxiety, depression), cognitive function or craving. PubMed and Embase, English only, 2014 to October 2023. 17 entries from 133 records are tabulated with sample size, type of exercise, duration, intensity, outcome measures and a one-line outcome; results are described in narrative form without numbers, effect sizes or appraisal results.
can_establish: Which exercise studies in people with methamphetamine use disorder were published in English in 2014 to 2023 and found in two databases, what they measured, and in which direction their authors reported results.
cannot_establish: How large any effect of exercise on mood, cognition or craving is (no numbers are extracted or pooled), how trustworthy the included studies are (no appraisal results; the tool named is meant for reviews, not studies), whether benefits last, whether exercise is safe for this group (no adverse-event data), or whether the findings apply outside compulsory or residential rehabilitation, mostly in China.

sample.recruitment: Databases PubMed and Embase; the included studies were done mostly in Chinese compulsory drug rehabilitation institutions, as the authors state, plus one US residential treatment trial reported three times.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: English; DSM-5 methamphetamine use disorder; clearly described physical activity as the intervention; quantifiable outcomes of negative mood, cognition or craving; 'prospective studies, randomized controlled trials, or intervention studies'. Excluded: 'insufficient evidence or very low quality', not focused on methamphetamine use disorder, animal or in-vitro studies, conference papers and reviews (2. Methodology, 3rd paragraph).
sample.demographics: Sample sizes 24 to 466; ages 18 to 45, mean mostly around 31; several studies in men only or women only (Table 1; Discussion, 2nd paragraph).
sample.attrition: Not reported for any included study.
sample.selection_effects: Two databases, English only, a 2014 to 2023 window, no grey literature, registries or reference-list searching; the review counts one 135-person US trial three times (Haglund 2015; Rawson 2015 in J Subst Abuse Treat, which is rawson_2015; Rawson 2015 in Drug Alcohol Depend) and includes a trial protocol (Menglu 2021, Trials) that has no results; one entry (Yin 2022) is titled as a study of people with substance use disorder generally.

exposure.measurement: Exercise programmes or single sessions delivered by the included studies; adherence not reported by the review.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions as tabulated (Table 1): single sessions of dancing, stationary cycling, treadmill or virtual-reality cycling lasting 10 to 35 minutes, at light, moderate or high intensity (refs 24, 25, 30, 32, 34); programmes of aerobic, resistance, high-intensity interval, Tai Chi or combined exercise, 24 to 60 minutes per session, three to five times a week, for 4 weeks to 6 months (refs 16, 22, 23, 26 to 29, 31, 33, 35 to 37). The review states that moderate-intensity exercise (refs 16, 24 to 27, 30, 31, 34, 37) and high-intensity interval training (refs 28, 29, 32) showed greater benefits, and that one acute study (ref 25, Wang 2016) found larger falls in craving with moderate and high than with low intensity. The text gives 20 minutes for the acute session in ref 30 where Table 1 gives 30 minutes.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Participants were in rehabilitation or residential treatment and abstinent by setting; verification is not described by the review.

comparison.controls: The Discussion says control groups received health education by watching materials or videos; individual comparators are not tabulated, and the acute studies used other designs.
comparison.matching: The Discussion states that exercise and control groups were matched for age and education; this is not shown for any study.

outcomes.instruments: As listed in Table 1: self-rating anxiety and depression scales, Beck Depression and Anxiety Inventories, MINI interview, quality of life, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index; Stroop, Go/No-Go, 2-back, Trail Making, digit span, CogState and other cognitive tasks; event-related potentials, near-infrared spectroscopy, heart-rate variability; visual analogue craving scales, the Desires for Drug Questionnaire and cue-induced craving; urine drug screens.
outcomes.operationalization: Improvement as described by each study's authors; no common outcome or threshold.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported. The methods say risk of bias was assessed by two reviewers with the AMSTAR 2 tool, which appraises systematic reviews rather than individual studies, and no assessment results appear.

analysis.effect_sizes: None. The review reports no numerical results from any included study and no pooled estimate; Table 1 gives one-line verbal outcomes (for example 'reduce depression and anxiety symptoms', 'craving score reduced').
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42024530359; the registration date is not given in the paper (search to October 2023; received 19 March 2024). The protocol was not read, so deviations cannot be judged.
analysis.selective_reporting: No numbers, appraisal results or excluded-study list are reported; one sentence on craving falling during and after exercise carries no citation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: A list of 17 entries (in fact at most 14 distinct studies with results, from at most 1326 participants by the editors' arithmetic) whose authors reported improvements in depression and anxiety, inhibitory control and executive function, and craving with exercise, given without numbers or appraisal.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the evidence showed exercise interventions "may be effective" for withdrawal symptoms; the Discussion speaks of "consistent evidence" and the Conclusion calls exercise a safe, accessible and effective intervention. Gaps: (1) effectiveness is asserted without any effect size or appraisal; (2) 'safe' rests on no adverse-event data; (3) the participant total double-counts one trial twice over and includes a protocol with no participants yet; (4) the control group of the US trial is twice described as a healthy control group, when it was people with methamphetamine dependence attending health education; (5) the Discussion's statements that participants received no treatment other than exercise and that groups were matched for age and education are not true of the residential trial and are not shown for the others.

timeline.event: Rawson et al., randomized trial of exercise against health education during residential treatment, depression and anxiety outcomes (one of three reports of the same trial in this review).

replication.where_it_stands: The review is an inventory, not a synthesis: claims may cite it for which studies exist and the direction their authors reported, never for effect sizes. Its one US trial is held separately as rawson_2015 and must not be counted twice.

funding.funder: Yunnan Technological Innovation Centre of Drug Addiction Medicine (202305AK340001); Yunnan Province Expert Workstation of Cangming Huang (202105AF150040); Yunnan Province Technology Industry Leading Talents Support Program; Yunnan Fundamental Research projects (202202AS070077, 202201AY070001-079, 202201AU070227); Yunnan Provincial Department of Education (2023J0011).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from institutions in Yunnan, China (drug addiction medicine).

what_would_settle_it: A registered systematic review with a full search (several databases, Chinese-language sources, registries), appraisal of each trial, extraction of numbers and a meta-analysis by outcome and timing, counting each trial once; and large randomized trials of exercise during early abstinence with blinded outcome assessment, adverse events and follow-up after discharge.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Four critical items are 'no' (4: search; 7: excluded studies; 9: appraisal of the included studies; 13: interpretation), with item 2 only partly met, which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence. Beyond the instrument, the review triple-counts one trial, includes a protocol as if it had results, and misdescribes the control group of its only US trial. It may be cited only as an inventory of studies and of the direction their authors reported; every effect claim should go to the primary studies.

key_findings.finding: 17 entries from 133 records were included and described as reporting results from 1836 participants with methamphetamine use disorder; sample sizes ranged from 24 to 466. Removing the two duplicate reports and the protocol (next finding) leaves at most 14 distinct studies with results.
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Methods; 2. Methodology, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Three of the 17 entries (refs 22, 23, 37: Haglund 2015; Rawson 2015, J Subst Abuse Treat; Rawson 2015, Drug Alcohol Depend) report the same 135-person US trial, and ref 29 (Menglu 2021, Trials) is a study protocol of 240 planned participants with no results, although Table 1 lists an outcome for it. Removing the duplicates and the protocol leaves at most 1326 participants with results (editors' arithmetic).

Mood: the review reports that exercise improved depression and anxiety in four entries (refs 16, 22, 23, 24), one of them a single dance session that reduced attention to negative stimuli in women; no numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.1 Negative emotions, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Craving: the review reports lower craving with exercise in six entries (refs 25, 30, 34, 35, 36, 37), including single sessions in which craving fell during and shortly after exercise compared with control conditions, and programmes of aerobic-plus-resistance exercise or Tai Chi; ref 37 reported less methamphetamine use after the programme among people with lower-severity use. No numbers are given.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.3 Drug cravings, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Cognition: improvements in inhibitory control (refs 25, 28 to 30, 33) and executive function (refs 26, 27) are reported in words only.
key_findings.locator: Results › 3.2 Cognitive performance, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Discussion, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: The methods say risk of bias was assessed by two independent reviewers using AMSTAR 2; no appraisal result for any study is reported.

The authors' limitations: few studies; inconsistent sex distribution, exercise types and control conditions; most studies from China because of its compulsory drug rehabilitation institutions. The conclusion calls exercise a safe, accessible and effective intervention, although no adverse events are reported.

reporting_issues.issue: The participant total (1836) is the sum of the 17 tabulated sample sizes, which counts the same 135-person trial three times and adds 240 people from a protocol that had not reported results.
reporting_issues.consequence: The evidence base is overstated by about 510 participants and two studies; the protocol's tabulated 'outcome' is not a result.

reporting_issues.issue: Rawson 2015's comparison group is described twice as 'healthy' (lower scores 'than healthy groups'; 'than in the healthy control group'), but it was a health-education control group of people with methamphetamine dependence in the same residential programme.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3.1 Negative emotions, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader would think exercised patients did better than healthy people; the comparison was with other patients.

reporting_issues.issue: The text describes ref 26 as a randomized trial of 330 people while Table 1 gives N = 466; for ref 30 the text and Table 1 give different session lengths (exposure field).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3.2 Cognitive performance, 3rd paragraph; Results › 3.3 Drug cravings, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: Basic study characteristics in the review cannot be relied on without the primary papers.

reporting_issues.issue: AMSTAR 2, an instrument for appraising systematic reviews, is named as the tool used to assess the included studies, and no results are given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The included studies were in effect not appraised.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref 28 (Yin 2022) is titled as a study of acute effects in people with substance use disorder generally, while Table 1 describes a six-month programme in men with methamphetamine use disorder; the review's DSM-5 eligibility criterion may not be met.
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one entry may be ineligible or misdescribed.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that participants received no treatment other than exercise and that exercise and control groups were matched for age and education; the US residential trial's participants were in residential treatment, and matching is not shown for any study.
reporting_issues.consequence: General statements about the included studies are unreliable.

reporting_issues.issue: A sentence reporting that craving fell during exercise and at two later measurements, below the control group, carries no reference.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › 3.3 Drug cravings, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The finding cannot be traced to a study.
